description: Pattern matching and term rewriting are the heart of the Wolfram Language: definitions are rules attached to symbols, and transformations are applied by matching structural patterns against expressions. This category covers the pattern constructs, the rule and replacement operators, and the assignment and clearing functions that create and remove definitions.

tools.name: Blank
tools.description: The basic pattern object, written _, matching any single expression. x_ names the matched expression x for use on the right-hand side, and _h restricts the match to expressions with head h, so x_Integer matches only integers. Blank is the building block of essentially every Wolfram Language definition.
tools.example:
MatchQ[5, _]
MatchQ[5, _Integer]
f[x_] := x^2;
f[7]
Cases[{1, a, 2.5}, _Real]
tools.notes: _h tests Head[expr] === h exactly, so _Real does not match the integer 2; use _?NumericQ or _?NumberQ for a broader numeric test.

tools.name: BlankSequence
tools.description: Written __ (two underscores), it matches a sequence of one or more expressions. x__ names the whole sequence, and x__h requires every element to have head h. It is how you write definitions that accept a variable number of arguments.
tools.notes: Inside the body, x refers to a Sequence, so wrap it as {x} to get a list. Use ___ (BlankNullSequence) when zero arguments must also match.

tools.name: BlankNullSequence
tools.description: Written ___ (three underscores), it matches a sequence of zero or more expressions. This is the pattern to use when trailing or optional arguments may be absent entirely, and it is the standard way to match 'anything else' in the middle of a list. ___h constrains the head of every matched element.
tools.notes: Patterns with ___ can match in many ways; Longest and Shortest control which alternative is preferred when it matters.

tools.name: Pattern
tools.description: Assigns a name to a pattern so the matched expression can be referred to on the right-hand side of a rule or definition. The colon syntax x:patt is the general form; x_ is shorthand for x:_ and x_h for x:_h. Naming is also what enforces consistency, since the same name must match the same expression throughout a pattern.
tools.usage:
x : patt
Pattern[x, patt]
x_
x_h
tools.notes: Repeating a name enforces equality: f[x_, x_] only matches when both arguments are identical.

tools.name: PatternTest
tools.description: Written patt?test, it matches only when applying the test function to the candidate gives True. It is the fast way to add a predicate such as NumericQ, Positive or PrimeQ to a pattern, and it is checked before the rule body is evaluated. The test must be a function name or pure function, not an expression involving the pattern variable.
tools.example:
Cases[{1, -2, 3.5}, _?Positive]
f[n_?IntegerQ] := n!;
f[5]
Cases[Range[20], _?(Mod[#, 3] == 0 &)]
MatchQ[{1, 2}, {__?NumberQ}]
tools.notes: ?, binds very tightly: _?f&&g parses unexpectedly, so parenthesize pure functions as _?(... &). Use Condition (/;) when the test involves several pattern variables.

tools.name: Condition
tools.description: Written lhs /; test, it makes a pattern or definition apply only when the test evaluates to True. Placed on a pattern it restricts matching; placed on the whole right-hand side of a definition it acts as a guard that can refer to all the pattern variables at once. Conditions are evaluated after a structural match succeeds, so the variables already have values.
tools.usage:
patt /; test
lhs :> rhs /; test
lhs := rhs /; test
tools.notes: If the condition is False the definition is treated as non-matching and evaluation falls through to other definitions, which is how multi-clause functions with guards are written.

tools.name: Alternatives
tools.description: Written p1 | p2 | ..., it matches any one of several patterns. It is used for enumerated options, for matching several heads at once, and for building small grammars in string and expression patterns. A name can be attached to the whole alternative with x:(p1 | p2).
tools.usage:
p1 | p2 | ...
Alternatives[p1, p2, ...]
x : (p1 | p2)
tools.example:
Cases[{1, a, "s", 2.0}, _Integer | _Real]
MatchQ["stop", "go" | "stop"]
f[x : (_Integer | _Rational)] := N[x];
ReplaceAll[{a, b, c}, a | c -> x]
tools.notes: Pattern names must be assigned outside the alternative, not inside separate branches, or the rule may not see a consistent binding.

tools.name: Optional
tools.description: Written patt:default, it makes an argument optional and supplies a default when it is absent. In a function definition f[x_, n_:1] gives n the value 1 when only one argument is supplied. A bare x_. uses the default value registered for the enclosing function through Default.
tools.usage:
patt : default
x_ : default
x_.
Optional[patt, default]
tools.example:
f[x_, n_: 2] := x^n;
f[3]
f[3, 3]
MatchQ[f[a], f[_, _: 0]]
ReplaceAll[a + b, x_. + b :> x]
tools.notes: Do not confuse x_:v (Optional) with x:patt (named Pattern); the difference is whether the left side is a blank or a name. Optional arguments must come after all required ones.

tools.name: Repeated
tools.description: Written patt.., it matches one or more occurrences of a pattern; RepeatedNull (patt...) matches zero or more. A second argument bounds the number of repetitions, e.g. Repeated[_Integer, {3}] for exactly three. It is the way to express 'a list of n things of this kind' without spelling them out.
tools.usage:
patt ..
patt ...
Repeated[patt, max]
Repeated[patt, {min, max}]
tools.example:
MatchQ[{1, 2, 3}, {_Integer ..}]
MatchQ[{}, {_Integer ...}]
MatchQ[{1, 2, 3}, {Repeated[_Integer, {3}]}]
Cases[{{1, 1}, {1, 2, 1}}, {1 ..}]
tools.notes: Repeated applies to the pattern immediately to its left; use parentheses for compound patterns, e.g. (a | b) ...

tools.name: PatternSequence
tools.description: Represents a sequence of patterns that must appear together as arguments, without introducing an extra level of list structure. It lets you name or repeat a group of arguments, for example matching coordinate pairs in a flat argument list. Combined with Repeated it expresses repeating groups.
tools.notes: PatternSequence[] matches nothing at all, which is useful as an 'absent' alternative in optional argument groups.

tools.name: Except
tools.description: Matches any expression that does not match a given pattern. Except[c, patt] first requires a match to patt and then excludes those that also match c, which is the way to say 'a number, but not zero'. It is the cleanest way to write negative conditions in Cases and DeleteCases.
tools.example:
Cases[{1, a, 2, b}, Except[_Integer]]
Cases[{0, 1, 2, 0}, Except[0, _Integer]]
DeleteCases[{1, "a", 2}, Except[_String]]
MatchQ[3, Except[1 | 2]]

tools.name: Longest
tools.description: Forces a pattern that could match different amounts to match as much as possible (greedy matching). It matters mainly for __ and ___ in expression patterns and for RegularExpression-style string patterns, where the default is greedy for strings but leftmost-shortest for some expression cases. Shortest is the complementary directive.
tools.example: StringCases["aaa", Longest["a" ..]] ReplaceAll[{1, 2, 3, 4}, {Longest[a__], b_} :> {a}] StringCases["x", Longest["<" ~~ __ ~~ ">"]]

tools.name: Shortest
tools.description: Forces a flexible pattern to match as little as possible (lazy matching). It is most often used in string patterns to stop a wildcard from swallowing everything up to the last delimiter, for example when extracting HTML tags or quoted fields. It has no effect on patterns that can only match one way.
tools.example:
StringCases["<a><b>", Shortest["<" ~~ x__ ~~ ">"] :> x]
StringReplace["a1b2c3", Shortest[__ ~~ "3"] -> "X"]
ReplaceAll[{1, 2, 3}, {Shortest[a___], b_} :> {a}]

tools.name: HoldPattern
tools.description: Wraps a pattern so that it is not evaluated when the enclosing rule or definition is created, while still matching the expression it contains. It is essential when the left-hand side of a rule would otherwise evaluate away, for example a pattern containing a defined symbol or an arithmetic expression. HoldPattern is invisible during matching, so it never changes what a pattern matches.
tools.notes: DownValues always display their left-hand sides wrapped in HoldPattern for exactly this reason. Verbatim is different: it prevents the contents being treated as a pattern at all.

tools.name: Verbatim
tools.description: Makes a pattern match an expression literally, including pattern constructs, instead of interpreting it as a pattern. Verbatim[_] matches the symbol Blank[] itself rather than anything. Use it when transforming rules, patterns or definitions as data.
tools.example:
Cases[{_, x_, 3}, Verbatim[_]]
MatchQ[x_, Verbatim[x_]]
ReplaceAll[{a_ -> b}, Verbatim[a_] -> z]
tools.notes: HoldPattern prevents evaluation but still treats the contents as a pattern; Verbatim treats the contents as a literal expression.

tools.name: Rule
tools.description: Written lhs -> rhs, it represents a transformation rule whose right-hand side is evaluated immediately when the rule is created. Rules are ordinary expressions passed to Replace, ReplaceAll and hundreds of built-in functions, and they are also the syntax for option settings. A list of rules is applied as a set of alternatives, with the first applicable rule winning.
tools.example:
x + y /. x -> 2
{a, b} /. {a -> 1, b -> 2}
Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}, PlotStyle -> Red]
Solve[x^2 == 4, x]
tools.notes: Use RuleDelayed (:>) when the right-hand side must be recomputed for each match or refers to pattern variables that should not evaluate early.

tools.name: RuleDelayed
tools.description: Written lhs :> rhs, it is a transformation rule whose right-hand side is held and only evaluated when the rule is applied. This matters whenever the right-hand side involves pattern variables, random numbers, side effects, or anything that must not be computed at rule-creation time. It is the rule analogue of SetDelayed.
tools.example:
{1, 2, 3} /. n_Integer :> n^2
{a, b, c} /. _ :> RandomInteger[10]
Cases[{f[1], f[2]}, f[n_] :> n + 1]
{x, y} /. s_Symbol :> SymbolName[s]
tools.notes: Using -> instead of :> with pattern variables is a common bug: the right-hand side evaluates once with the variables still symbolic.

tools.name: Replace
tools.description: Applies rules to an expression as a whole rather than to its parts, returning the original unchanged if nothing matches. A level specification makes it act on subexpressions at chosen levels, and Replace[expr, rules, All] covers every level including the top. It is the precise tool when you want exactly one replacement at a known level.
tools.usage:
Replace[expr, rules]
Replace[expr, rules, levelspec]
Replace[rules][expr]
tools.example:
Replace[{1, 2}, {a_, b_} :> a + b]
Replace[x^2, x^n_ :> n]
Replace[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, {a_, b_} :> a, {1}]
Replace[f[x], _ -> done]
tools.notes: Replace only tries the top level by default, which is the main difference from ReplaceAll (/.) that tries every subexpression.

tools.name: ReplaceAll
tools.description: Written expr /. rules, it applies rules to every subexpression, scanning from the top down and not re-examining parts that have already been replaced. It is the everyday substitution operator, used for plugging values into formulas and for applying the rule lists returned by Solve. Each subexpression is transformed at most once per pass.
tools.example:
x^2 + y /. x -> 3
Sin[x] /. x -> Pi/2
sol = Solve[x^2 == 2, x];
x /. sol
{1, 2, 3} /. n_Integer :> n^2
tools.notes: Rules are tried in order at each subexpression; since replacement is not repeated, use //. (ReplaceRepeated) when the result may itself need transforming.

tools.name: ReplaceRepeated
tools.description: Written expr //. rules, it applies rules over and over until the expression stops changing, implementing a small rewrite system. Use it for simplification rule sets, symbolic normalization and recursive expansions. The MaxIterations option (default 65536) guards against non-terminating rule sets.
tools.usage:
expr //. rules
ReplaceRepeated[expr, rules]
ReplaceRepeated[expr, rules, MaxIterations -> n]
tools.notes: A rule whose output matches its own input loops forever until MaxIterations; FixedPoint with an explicit test gives more control.

tools.name: ReplaceList
tools.description: Returns a list of all the different results obtainable by applying rules to an expression in every possible way. It is the tool for exploring the non-deterministic choices in a flexible pattern, such as all the ways to split a sequence. An optional count limits how many results are produced.
tools.example:
ReplaceList[{a, b, c}, {x___, y___} :> {{x}, {y}}]
ReplaceList[a + b + c, x_ + y_ :> {x, y}]
ReplaceList[{1, 2, 3, 4}, {a___, b_, c___} :> b, 2]
tools.notes: Very useful for understanding why a flexible pattern matched a particular way, and for combinatorial enumeration by rewriting.

tools.name: MatchQ
tools.description: Tests whether an expression matches a pattern, returning True or False. It is the direct way to validate arguments, to filter with Select, and to debug patterns interactively. The operator form MatchQ[patt] is convenient inside Map and Select.
tools.example:
MatchQ[5, _Integer]
MatchQ[{1, 2, 3}, {__Integer}]
MatchQ[f[1, 2], f[_, _]]
Select[{f[1], g[2], f[3]}, MatchQ[f[_]]]
tools.notes: MatchQ evaluates its first argument before matching, so use Hold or HoldPattern when testing unevaluated forms.

tools.name: DeleteCases
tools.description: Removes every element matching a pattern, the complement of Cases. A level specification reaches into nested structures and a count limits how many elements are removed. It is the standard way to strip out Missing values, options, zeros or other unwanted elements.
tools.usage:
DeleteCases[expr, pattern]
DeleteCases[expr, pattern, levelspec]
DeleteCases[expr, pattern, levelspec, n]
tools.example:
DeleteCases[{1, a, 2, b}, _Symbol]
DeleteCases[{1, 0, 2, 0}, 0]
DeleteCases[{{1, x}, {2, y}}, _Symbol, 2]
DeleteCases[data, _Missing, Infinity]
tools.notes: DeleteMissing is a dedicated shortcut for dropping Missing entries from lists and Associations.

tools.name: FirstCase
tools.description: Returns the first element matching a pattern, with an optional default for when nothing matches, stopping the search as soon as a match is found. It replaces the common First[Cases[...]] idiom and is much faster on long lists. A level specification allows deep searching.
tools.usage:
FirstCase[expr, pattern]
FirstCase[expr, pattern, default]
FirstCase[expr, pattern, default, levelspec]
tools.example:
FirstCase[{1, a, 2}, _Symbol]
FirstCase[{1, 2, 3}, _String, "none"]
FirstCase[expr, _Integer, Missing[], Infinity]
FirstCase[Range[100], _?(# > 50 &)]
tools.notes: Without a default, no match gives Missing["NotFound"]. FirstPosition is the positional analogue.

tools.name: Set
tools.description: Written lhs = rhs, it evaluates the right-hand side once and assigns the result. For a plain symbol this creates an OwnValue; for a pattern like f[x_] it creates a DownValue whose body is already evaluated. Set is also used to modify parts of an expression in place, as in m[[2, 3]] = 0.
tools.usage:
lhs = rhs
Set[lhs, rhs]
{a, b} = {1, 2}
expr[[i]] = value
tools.notes: Use = for values computed once and := for definitions that must be recomputed on each call. Assignment to a Protected symbol fails with a message until Unprotect is used.

tools.name: SetDelayed
tools.description: Written lhs := rhs, it stores the right-hand side unevaluated and re-evaluates it each time the left-hand side matches. This is the normal way to define functions, because the body must be evaluated with the arguments substituted. SetDelayed has attribute HoldAll and returns Null, so nothing is printed when a definition is made.
tools.usage:
lhs := rhs
SetDelayed[lhs, rhs]
f[x_] := body
f[x_] := body /; condition
tools.notes: A memoizing definition combines both: f[n_] := f[n] = expensive[n] stores each computed value as a new rule.

tools.name: TagSet
tools.description: Written f /: lhs = rhs (or /: ... := ...), it attaches a definition to the symbol f named as the tag rather than to the head of the left-hand side. This is how you add rules for your own symbol to built-in operations such as Plus, Times or Format without unprotecting them. The tag must appear somewhere in the left-hand side.
tools.usage:
f /: lhs = rhs
f /: lhs := rhs
TagSet[f, lhs, rhs]
tools.notes: TagSet with the tag equal to the head of the left-hand side is the same as an ordinary definition; with a tag deeper inside it creates an UpValue on that symbol.

tools.name: UpSet
tools.description: Written lhs ^= rhs (and ^:= for the delayed form), it defines a rule stored with the symbols that appear as arguments of the left-hand side rather than with its head. This lets a user-defined object participate in built-in operations: defining Plus[myThing[a_], myThing[b_]] ^:= ... attaches the rule to myThing. UpValues are checked before the built-in behaviour of the enclosing function.
tools.usage:
lhs ^= rhs
lhs ^:= rhs
UpSet[lhs, rhs]
tools.notes: UpSet attaches the rule to every symbol appearing at level 1 of the left-hand side; use TagSet (/:) to control exactly which symbol carries it.

tools.name: Clear
tools.description: Removes the values and definitions associated with symbols, while keeping their attributes, options, messages and the symbols themselves. String arguments with metacharacters clear whole groups, so Clear["Global`*"] wipes the user's definitions in a session. It is the usual first line of a notebook cell that redefines a function.
tools.notes: Clear does not remove attributes such as Protected or Listable; ClearAll does. Clearing a Protected built-in requires Unprotect first.

tools.name: ClearAll
tools.description: Removes all values, definitions, attributes, options, messages and defaults from symbols, returning them to a pristine state. Use it when a symbol has acquired attributes such as Listable or HoldAll that must also go. It accepts the same string patterns as Clear for clearing whole contexts.
tools.notes: ClearAll leaves the symbol itself in the context; use Remove to delete the symbol entirely.

tools.name: Remove
tools.description: Completely removes symbols from the system, so their names are no longer recognized and can be reused for a fresh symbol. This is stronger than ClearAll and is the fix for shadowing problems, where the same short name exists in two contexts. Anything still referring to the removed symbol displays it as Removed["name"].
tools.notes: Remove existing expressions that still contain the symbol become invalid, which is why it is normally used only for cleaning up contexts before reloading a package.

tools.name: Unset
tools.description: Written lhs =., it removes the single definition whose left-hand side matches lhs, leaving other definitions for the same symbol in place. Use it to retract one specific rule from a multi-clause function. Unsetting something that has no definition produces a message unless the pattern is used.
tools.notes: To remove every definition at once use Clear; to remove a parameterized rule you must give the exact same pattern, e.g. f[x_] =.

tools.name: DownValues
tools.description: Gives the list of transformation rules defined for a symbol when it appears as the head of an expression, i.e. the ordinary function definitions. The rules are returned as HoldPattern[lhs] :> rhs, and the list can be reordered or assigned back to change or reorder definitions. It is the main tool for inspecting and manipulating definitions programmatically.
tools.notes: Memoized definitions accumulate in DownValues and can consume memory; Clear[f] discards them. Use Definition[f] for a human-readable printout of everything attached to f.

tools.name: OwnValues
tools.description: Gives the rule that defines the value of a symbol used on its own, as created by x = 5 or x := expr. The result is a single HoldPattern[x] :> value rule, or {} for a symbol with no value. Use it to inspect a variable's definition without triggering its evaluation.
tools.notes: OwnValues has attribute HoldAll, so the symbol is not evaluated before being examined.

tools.name: UpValues
tools.description: Gives the rules attached to a symbol that apply when it appears inside another function, as created by UpSet (^=) or TagSet (/:). These rules let user objects extend built-in operations without modifying protected symbols. Like DownValues, the list can be read, reordered and assigned.
tools.notes: UpValues are consulted before the built-in definitions of the enclosing head, which makes them the safe way to overload Plus, Times or Norm for your own types.

tools.name: Default
tools.description: Specifies the default value used when an optional argument written x_. is omitted for a given function. Default[f] = v sets one default for all argument positions, and Default[f, i] sets it for position i. Built-in defaults exist for Plus (0), Times (1) and Power (1), which is why patterns like a_. x match a bare x.
tools.usage:
Default[f] = v
Default[f, i] = v
Default[f, i, n] = v
tools.notes: Defaults only apply to the x_. shorthand; the explicit Optional form x_:v carries its own default and does not consult Default.
